title: Modelling lock-in of AI adoption through skill erosion
title_zh: 通过技能侵蚀建模AI采纳的锁定效应

paragraphs.en: Generative AI can improve immediate performance but may erode the human skills required for future work. We study a model in which individuals tend to imitate successful peers, while their independent skills grow with practice and erode with reliance on AI. Because each agent’s skill reflects their history, non-users and AI users develop different skill distributions, which we derive exactly. Skill erosion can produce bistability and hysteresis between a low-adoption, high-skill state and a high-adoption, low-skill state. When agents rarely change behaviour at random, the two transitions are asymmetric. A single AI user spreads through a population of experts only if AI-assisted work earns more than expert work, whatever the timescale of skill adaptation. A single non-user, by contrast, can lead an AI-dependent population back to independent work only if they regain enough skill before returning to AI, which becomes easier the more persistent behaviours are. As AI improves, adoption can jump abruptly, and a sufficiently long increase in its benefit, such as a period of low prices, can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. Skill erosion thus creates a history-dependent switching cost that can make widespread AI adoption difficult to reverse.

paragraphs.en: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly becoming part of how people write, code, learn and make decisions. It can improve immediate performance in a wide range of tasks, but it can also reduce performance at two levels. At the individual level, relying on AI may reduce the practice that maintains one’s capacity to work independently: AI assistance can help with a task yet reduce persistence and subsequent independent performance [ 1 ] . Whether assistance supports or harms learning also depends on how it engages the user [ 2 , 3 ] . At the collective level, the value of AI-assisted work may decrease as more people rely on the same tools [ 4 ] . Their outputs become more similar, reducing the diversity of ideas and content [ 5 , 6 ] , much as navigation services that give the same advice to many drivers concentrate traffic on the same roads [ 7 ] . AI systems retrained on increasingly synthetic data can also progressively lose quality, a phenomenon known as model collapse [ 8 , 9 ] . The adoption of AI is, moreover, a social process, as for any technology [ 10 ] . A software developer adopting a code assistant, a student solving exercises with a chatbot and an analyst drafting reports with a language model all observe how well these tools serve their peers, and may be encouraged to adopt them when others appear to benefit.

paragraphs.en: Models of social learning and evolutionary game theory provide a natural framework for such adoption dynamics [ 11 , 12 ] . In conventional models, the payoff of a strategy depends on current strategies, but not on the history of the individual who plays it. AI adoption differs, as every individual carries an internal state, their skill, which evolves with their own behavioural history: using AI changes the skill of the user, and therefore the payoff of their future decisions. Coevolutionary games, in which strategies coevolve with individual attributes [ 13 ] , come closest to this setting. We call the dependence of an agent’s skill, and hence of the payoff of their next choice, on their own history of actions individual memory . Two AI users can have the same behaviour at a given moment, while one, who has just adopted AI, retains the expertise of years of independent practice, and the other, who has relied on AI for a long time, has lost it. It is thus not memory in the sense of repeated games, in which strategies condition on past moves, but the impact that an agent’s past behaviour leaves on their own skill.

paragraphs.en: In this article, we show that the erosion of skills can make the adoption of AI abrupt and hard to reverse, in a minimal model with an exact stationary solution and two competing feedbacks 1 1 1 A recent preprint by Frigerio et al. [ 22 ] , posted while this work was in preparation, independently studied a closely related model and also reported bistability and hysteresis, a narrowing of the bistable region with increasing timescale ratio, and skill polarisation, including different skill distributions at fixed adoption and mean skill. Their weak-selection, covariance-closure analysis gives an effective-feedback coefficient that decreases with the timescale ratio; their main text uses a Beta law as an analytical approximation to the skill-dependent agent-based model. Their Supplementary Information derives Beta distributions for skill-independent switching and a zero-flux stationary density, with a weak-selection correction, for skill-dependent Fermi switching. The present work follows a different analytical route: it uses a linear pairwise comparison to obtain explicit self-consistent stationary distributions at finite selection, and it develops a lone-holdout invasion criterion and simulations of finite-duration changes in AI’s benefit. . Relying on AI raises immediate productivity but erodes independent skill, which makes AI relatively more attractive and reinforces adoption, whereas widespread adoption leads to a loss of distinctiveness and reduces the advantage of AI-assisted work. As each agent’s skill reflects their own history, non-users and AI users form two populations with different distributions of skill, and the rate at which agents move from one to the other depends on their skill. We derive the stationary skill distributions exactly, allowing us to determine how individual histories affect collective AI adoption and the conditions under which different adoption regimes coexist. When skill erosion outweighs crowding, a state of low adoption and high skill and a state of high adoption and low skill can coexist, with hysteresis between them, and the relative timescales of skill adaptation and behavioural change determine the range of benefits of AI over which they do. Note that tipping points, hysteresis and irreversible dependence on AI have also been obtained in population-level models [ 14 , 15 ] , where capability is described by population averages or compartments, whereas here each agent carries their own skill.

paragraphs.en: Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for lock-in. Skill erosion acts as a switching cost, a classic source of lock-in in economics [ 17 , 18 ] , but one that is borne through the user’s own eroded capability and grows with the length of use. Simulations of a benefit of AI that rises and then falls, e.g. when a period of low prices ends, show that adoption can jump abruptly as AI improves, that a temporary increase in its benefit locks a population in if it lasts long enough, and that adoption alone does not reveal whether a population is locked in.
paragraphs.zh: 最后，我们讨论了我们的研究结果对锁定问题的启示。 技能侵蚀构成一种转换成本——这是经济学中经典的锁定来源 [17, 18]——但这种成本由用户自身被侵蚀的能力所承担，并随着使用时间的增长而增加。 对一种先升后降的 AI 收益（例如当低价期结束时）的模拟表明：随着 AI 的改进，采用率可能突然跃升；收益的暂时性提高若持续足够长的时间，会将一个群体锁定；而仅凭采用本身并不能揭示一个群体是否被锁定。

paragraphs.en: Figure 1 (b,c) illustrates the two regimes for a single agent: when the agent changes behaviour often, their skill stays close to its mean, whereas when their behaviour is persistent, it alternates between expertise and deep erosion. The correlation between current behaviour and skill, through which individual memory shapes collective behaviour, is strongest for large ρ \rho , when skill closely follows behaviour. As ρ → 0 \rho\to 0 , rapid switching averages over many behaviours before skill can adapt, so current behaviour carries little information about an agent’s skill. A large ρ \rho has two consequences, which we derive below: agents who stop using AI regain skill before they switch again, which weakens lock-in, whereas AI users lose theirs, which polarises skills. Linear payoffs, relaxation and imitation are the simplest choices that keep the two feedbacks of Fig. 1 (a); other choices are possible, and we discuss them in Sec. VI .

paragraphs.en: These distributions reveal a polarisation of skills that averages hide. As non-users pull their skill towards 1 1 and AI users towards 0 0 , the mean skill S S of the population obeys S ˙ = ε ⁡ ( 1 − x − S ) \dot{S}=\varepsilon(1-x-S) exactly (Appendix A ), so that S = 1 − x S=1-x at stationarity: adoption alone fixes the mean skill. Figure 2 illustrates this polarisation for populations tuned to the same adoption, x = 0.4 x=0.4 , and thus to the same mean skill, 0.6 0.6 , in a regime with a single stable state. As ρ \rho increases from 0.039 0.039 to 3.9 3.9 , the distribution of skills changes from a narrow peak around the mean to a U-shaped distribution, with non-users close to s = 1 s=1 and AI users close to s = 0 s=0 . The fraction of agents whose independent skill is below 0.2 0.2 rises from 0.00 0.00 to 0.10 0.10 and 0.33 0.33 , i.e. a third of the population has lost most of its capacity for independent work, while adoption and mean skill are unchanged. The exact densities agree with the histograms in all three regimes. In all three panels, AI users and non-users earn the same on average, within 0.011 0.011 , as required by Eq. ( 6 ): at ρ = 3.9 \rho=3.9 , AI users, whose mean independent skill is 0.12 0.12 , earn as much as non-users, whose mean skill is 0.92 0.92 . paragraphs.en: The coexistence of several self-consistent stationary states raises the questions of which are stable and how transitions between them occur; we examine these questions in the next section.

paragraphs.en: Having determined the stationary distributions of skill, we now ask which levels of AI adoption are possible and how they change with the benefit of AI. Two feedbacks compete: skill erosion makes AI relatively more attractive as adoption grows, whereas crowding makes it less attractive. When crowding dominates, or when behaviour is persistent enough, the population settles in a single state, whose adoption increases continuously with the benefit of AI. When skill erosion dominates, two stable states may coexist, one with low adoption and high skill and the other with high adoption and low skill, separated by an unstable state. As the benefit of AI changes, one of these states can disappear, leading to an abrupt transition and hysteresis.
paragraphs.zh: 在确定了技能的平稳分布之后，我们现在追问哪些 AI 采用水平是可能的，以及它们如何随 AI 收益的变化而改变。 两种反馈相互竞争：技能侵蚀使得 AI 在采用增长时相对更具吸引力，而拥挤效应则使其吸引力下降。 当拥挤效应占主导，或当行为具有足够的持续性时，种群会稳定在单一状态，该状态的采用水平随 AI 收益连续增加。 当技能侵蚀占主导时，可能共存两个稳定状态：一个是低采用、高技能的状态，另一个是高采用、低技能的状态，两者之间由一个不稳定状态分隔。 随着 AI 收益的变化，其中一个状态可能消失，从而导致突变和滞后效应。

paragraphs.en: So far, we have considered stationary states at a fixed benefit of AI. In practice, this benefit changes over time as tools improve or become more expensive. We now ask how quickly such changes affect adoption, and whether a temporary advantage can produce lasting dependence on AI. We investigate two scenarios: a benefit b b that increases and then decreases at a constant rate r r [Fig. 4 (a)], and a temporary increase in b b lasting for a duration D D [Fig. 4 (b)]. Details of the simulations are given in Appendix C .
paragraphs.zh: 到目前为止，我们考虑的是在 AI 收益固定的情况下的稳态。 在实践中，随着工具的改进或变得更加昂贵，这一收益会随时间变化。 我们现在追问：这样的变化会多快影响采用，以及暂时的优势是否能产生对 AI 的持久依赖。 我们考察两种情景：先以恒定速率 r r 上升然后下降的收益 b b [图 4 (a)]，以及持续时间为 D D 的 b b 暂时性上升 [图 4 (b)]。 模拟的细节见附录 C。

paragraphs.en: First, the speed of change matters. As AI improves, adoption remains low until the benefit crosses the upper stationary fold, after which it rises abruptly. Faster increases delay the transition because a small minority of AI users needs time to grow. On the way down, adoption remains high well below the benefit at which it rose, and the return to independent work is likewise delayed. The faster the changes, the wider the hysteresis observed for the rates considered [Fig. 4 (a)]. In the infinite-population adiabatic limit, r → 0 r\to 0 , the trajectories follow the stable stationary branches and jump at their folds, recovering the hysteresis loop of Fig. 3 (a), with transitions at b = 0.845 b=0.845 and 0.610 0.610 . For a finite population, this description applies only while the ramp is fast compared with the rare fluctuations that allow escape from a stable state. For illustration, if agents reconsider their use of AI about once a week, so that skills adapt over about five weeks, increasing b b from 0.3 0.3 to 1.15 1.15 takes about five years for r = 3 × 10 − 3 r=3\times 10^{-3} and one and a half years for r = 10 − 2 r=10^{-2} .

paragraphs.en: In this article, we have studied a model of the coevolution between AI adoption and human skills with an exact stationary solution. Its central mechanism is simple: relying on AI can improve immediate performance while eroding the skills needed to work independently, making further reliance on AI more attractive. This feedback can produce bistability and hysteresis: adoption may increase abruptly as AI improves, and even a temporary increase in its benefit can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value. We derived the stationary distributions of skill for non-users and AI users, showing that populations with the same adoption and mean skill can have very different distributions of expertise.

sents.en: In this article, we have studied a model of the coevolution between AI adoption and human skills with an exact stationary solution.
sents.zh: 在本文中，我们研究了一个AI采用与人类技能共同演化的模型，该模型具有精确的平稳解。

sents.en: Its central mechanism is simple: relying on AI can improve immediate performance while eroding the skills needed to work independently, making further reliance on AI more attractive.
sents.zh: 其核心机制很简单：依赖AI可以提升眼前的表现，但同时会削弱独立工作所需的技能，从而使进一步依赖AI变得更具吸引力。

sents.en: This feedback can produce bistability and hysteresis: adoption may increase abruptly as AI improves, and even a temporary increase in its benefit can leave a population relying on AI after the benefit has returned to its initial value.
sents.zh: 这种反馈可以产生双稳态和滞后效应：随着AI的改进，采用率可能突然上升，而且即使其收益只是暂时性提高，也可能在收益回落到初始值之后，仍然让群体保持对AI的依赖。

sents.en: We derived the stationary distributions of skill for non-users and AI users, showing that populations with the same adoption and mean skill can have very different distributions of expertise.
sents.zh: 我们推导了非用户与AI用户的技能平稳分布，表明具有相同采用率和平均技能的群体，其专业技能分布可能截然不同。

paragraphs.en: An important finding is that skill erosion and the persistence of behaviour play distinct roles. Skill erosion reinforces the adoption of AI, whereas the persistence of individual behaviours allows those who stop using AI to recover their skills before switching back. When exploration is rare, persistence therefore leaves unchanged the threshold at which AI invades a population of experts, but it makes the return to independent work easier. More generally, increasing this persistence narrows the bistable region, but also increases the polarisation of skills between AI users and non-users. Skill erosion thus acts as a history-dependent switching cost, different from the investments in equipment or workflows usually considered in economics [ 18 ] . The cost emerges through the loss of the user’s own capabilities, and adoption rates alone cannot reveal how far a population is locked into reliance on AI.
paragraphs.zh: 一个重要发现是，技能侵蚀和行为的持续性发挥着不同的作用。 技能侵蚀会强化对AI的采用，而个体行为的持续性则使停止使用AI的人能够在切换回AI之前恢复自己的技能。 因此，当探索很少发生时，持续性不会改变AI侵入专家群体的阈值，但它使回归独立工作变得更容易。 更一般地说，提高这种持续性会缩小双稳态区域，但也会加剧AI使用者与非使用者之间的技能两极分化。 因此，技能侵蚀起到了一种依赖历史的切换成本的作用，不同于经济学中通常考虑的设备或工作流程投资[ 18 ]。 这种成本是通过使用者自身能力的丧失而产生的，仅凭采用率无法揭示一个群体在多大程度上被锁定在对AI的依赖之中。

paragraphs.en: Several extensions would bring the model closer to real-world settings. Individuals differ in their skills, tasks and learning rates, and interact through social networks rather than uniformly with the population. The quality and price of AI may also respond to adoption, while users and providers may anticipate the long-term effects of their decisions. Most importantly, the model has not yet been calibrated against data. Following individuals’ AI use and their performance both with and without assistance would allow its predictions to be tested, particularly the relationship between the persistence of behaviour and the polarisation of independent skills. More generally, our results suggest that understanding the long-term consequences of AI adoption requires measuring not only how many people use AI, but also how their ability to work without it evolves.
